article.title: Why Difference-in-Differences Needs Parallel Trends, Not Just a Control Group
article.why: 理解 DiD 的核心識別假設，而非把有對照組誤當成因果保證。
article.author: OpenAI learning editor

paragraphs.en:
Difference-in-differences, often called DiD, is popular because its basic calculation is intuitive. We observe a treatment group and a comparison group before and after an intervention. We calculate the change in the treatment group, subtract the change in the comparison group, and interpret the remaining difference as the treatment effect. But simply having a control group does not make that interpretation valid.

The central identifying assumption is usually called parallel trends. It asks a counterfactual question: if the treatment had not happened, would the average outcome in the treated group have changed over time in a way that was comparable to the control group? The two groups do not need to start at the same level. They need a credible relationship in their untreated trends.

Imagine two regions. Before a marketing campaign, Region A has a conversion rate of 5 percent and Region B has 3 percent. After the campaign is introduced only in A, the rates become 7 percent and 4 percent. A increased by two percentage points while B increased by one, so the DiD estimate is one percentage point. Different starting levels are not automatically a problem.

However, suppose Region A had already been growing much faster than Region B for several months before the campaign. Then some of the extra post-campaign growth might simply continue that earlier pattern. A control group exists, but it may not represent what would have happened to A without treatment.

Pre-treatment data are therefore extremely valuable. Analysts often plot outcomes for several periods before intervention and examine whether the groups moved similarly. Event-study specifications can show estimated differences relative to treatment timing and reveal obvious pre-trends. These checks do not prove the assumption, because the untreated post-treatment path is never observed, but they can expose serious contradictions.

Another threat is a simultaneous shock. If Region A launches the campaign at the same time that a competitor closes stores there, the observed change may reflect both events. DiD removes common time shocks affecting both groups, but it cannot automatically remove a shock that affects only the treated group at the treatment date.

Composition can also change. If the customers observed in A after treatment are systematically different from those observed before treatment, the outcome shift may partly reflect population change. Depending on the setting, analysts may use balanced panels, repeated cross-sections with controls, weighting, or other designs to address observable composition differences.

Treatment timing requires care when different units adopt treatment at different dates. Simple two-way fixed-effects models can behave unexpectedly when treatment effects vary across groups or over time. Modern DiD methods explicitly account for staggered adoption and define appropriate comparison groups. The basic intuition remains useful, but the estimator must match the design.

Good analysis begins before regression. Write down who receives treatment, when it begins, what outcome is measured, and why the proposed comparison group is a credible counterfactual. Plot raw trends. Mark other policy or business changes on the timeline. Ask whether anticipation could change behavior before the official treatment date.

Communication should also separate evidence from assumptions. Instead of saying, “We had a control group, so the campaign caused a one-point increase,” say that the estimate has a causal interpretation under a parallel-trends assumption and after considering treatment-specific concurrent shocks. This wording makes the logic auditable.

DiD is powerful because it can remove stable differences between groups and common changes over time. Yet those strengths do not eliminate the need for a credible counterfactual. The method works not because one group is labeled control, but because its evolution helps approximate the untreated path of the treated group. That is the real question behind parallel trends.
paragraphs.zh: DiD 的關鍵不是「有 control group」，而是該組能否合理代表 treatment group 在沒有介入時的時間趨勢。應檢查 pre-trends、同步衝擊、構成變化、anticipation 與 staggered adoption。
paragraphs.ja: 差の差法では対照群が存在するだけでは不十分で、介入がなかった場合の処置群の推移を対照群が妥当に近似できるという平行トレンドの考え方が重要です。

Observe outcomes before and after intervention.
Anticipation may affect behavior before treatment.

grammar.title: would have + past participle
grammar.body: 用於描述未發生的反事實。例：What would have happened without treatment?

business.term: Do the pre-treatment trends support this comparison?
business.example: Before interpreting causally, do the pre-treatment trends support this comparison?

business.term: What else changed at the treatment date?
business.example: Let's list what else changed at the treatment date.

quiz.question: Do treatment and control groups need the same starting outcome level?
quiz.answer: No. DiD mainly requires a credible relationship in their untreated trends, not identical starting levels.
